Priya Lindqvist

From Openpedia, the free encyclopedia
Swedish entrepreneur (born 1988)
Not to be confused with another person of a similar name.
Priya Lindqvist
Born9 September 1988, Uppsala
OccupationEntrepreneur
Lindqvist in 2019

Priya Lindqvist (born 9 September 1988) is a Swedish entrepreneur who is the co-founder and chief executive of Meridel, a company that processes card and bank payments for online shops.[1][2] She founded the company in 2010 with her brother.[3]

Early life

[edit]

Lindqvist was born in Uppsala and grew up in a village north of the city, where her parents ran a small guest house.[4] She began to write computer programs at the age of ten on a machine that the guest house used for bookings.[5][6]

At sixteen she won a national science prize for a program that learned to sort handwritten forms.[7] She started a degree in mathematics at the University of Lund in 2007 and left before finishing it.[8]

Her first company made tools for sellers on auction websites, and she sold it in 2008 for about 5 million dollars while she was still a student.[9][10]

Career

[edit]

Meridel began as a few lines of code that a shop owner could paste into a website to take a card payment.[11] The service opened to the public in 2011 after a year of private testing with about fifty shops.[12][13]

The company raised 20 million dollars in 2012 from a group of investors that included two founders of earlier payment firms.[14][15] It opened offices in Berlin and Singapore in 2015.[16]

In 2016 a funding round valued Meridel at 9 billion dollars, which made Lindqvist and her brother two of the youngest billionaires in the country.[17][18]

Meridel employed about 7,000 people in 2023 and processed payments for shops in more than forty countries.[19][20]

Personal life

[edit]

Lindqvist lives in Stockholm and has said that she reads a book a week, mostly history and biography.[21] She learned to fly small aircraft in 2014 and holds a commercial pilot's licence.[22]

She co-founded a research institute in 2021 that pays for laboratory space and salaries for early-career scientists.[23][24]

She sits on the boards of two charities that fund school libraries in rural districts.[25]
